questions.question: What is RPO and how does it differ from RTO?
questions.answer: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time — it defines how old your most recent backup can be when disaster strikes. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable downtime — how long your system can be offline before it must be restored. RPO answers 'how much data can I lose?' and RTO answers 'how long can I be down?'. Both are set by the business based on cost tolerance.

questions.question: What is Amazon Route 53 and what are its four main functions?
questions.answer: Amazon Route 53 is AWS's highly available and scalable DNS and traffic routing service, named after DNS port 53. Its four functions are: (1) Domain Registration — register domain names directly through AWS; (2) DNS Resolution — translate domain names to IP addresses; (3) Health Checking — monitor endpoints and remove unhealthy ones from DNS responses; (4) Traffic Routing — apply intelligent routing rules (by latency, weight, location, etc.) to direct traffic.

questions.question: Explain the end-to-end DNS resolution process when a user types www.example.com in their browser.
questions.answer: 1. Browser checks local cache; if not cached, sends query to the DNS Resolver (ISP). 2. Resolver queries a DNS Root Name Server, which knows which TLD servers handle .com. 3. Root server responds: go to the .com TLD name server. 4. Resolver queries the TLD server: who is authoritative for example.com? 5. TLD server responds with Route 53 name servers. 6. Resolver queries Route 53, which returns the IP address (e.g., CloudFront CDN). 7. Resolver returns IP to the browser. 8. Browser connects to the CDN/server. 9. Content is delivered. The resolver caches the response for the duration of the record's TTL.

questions.question: What is TTL in DNS and why would you lower it before a planned migration?
questions.answer: TTL (Time to Live) is the duration in seconds for which DNS resolvers cache a DNS response. While the cache is valid, resolvers serve the cached IP without querying again. Before a planned migration, you lower TTL (e.g., from 3600 seconds to 60 seconds) so that after you update the DNS record, the change propagates quickly worldwide — resolvers will re-query after just 60 seconds instead of 1 hour.

questions.question: What is the difference between a public and private hosted zone in Route 53?
questions.answer: A public hosted zone routes DNS traffic from the internet to your resources — any user worldwide can resolve names in it. A private hosted zone routes DNS traffic only within one or more associated VPCs — it's used for internal service discovery within a corporate network or microservices environment. Internal resources like database.internal or api.internal are registered in private hosted zones.

questions.question: Name the seven Route 53 routing policies and give a one-sentence use case for each.
questions.answer: 1. Simple — single resource, all clients get the same response. 2. Weighted — distribute traffic by percentage, used for A/B testing or canary deployments. 3. Geolocation — route by user's geographic location, used for compliance or localised content. 4. Latency — route to the AWS Region with lowest network latency, used for best global performance. 5. Failover — active-passive disaster recovery, automatically switches to backup when primary fails. 6. Multivalue Answer — return up to 8 healthy IPs randomly, lightweight DNS load balancing. 7. IP-based — route by client CIDR IP range, used for network-specific routing.

questions.question: Which Route 53 routing policy does NOT support health checks and what is the risk of using it for a critical application?
questions.answer: Simple Routing does not support health checks. The risk is that if your single resource fails, Route 53 will still return its IP address — users will be directed to a broken server with no automatic failover. For critical applications, use Failover routing with health checks instead, which automatically removes unhealthy resources from DNS responses.

questions.question: Explain the difference between Blue/Green and Canary deployments. When would you choose each?
questions.answer: Blue/Green maintains two complete environments and switches 100% of traffic instantly from old (Blue) to new (Green). Rollback is instant. Cost is high (two full environments). Best for major releases where you need clean rollback and full pre-production testing. Canary gradually shifts a small percentage of traffic (e.g., 5%) to the new version using weighted routing, letting real users test it before full rollout. Cost is lower (new env starts small). Best for small features or risky updates where you want real-user validation with minimal blast radius.

questions.question: What AWS services would you recommend to achieve near-zero RPO for a relational database?
questions.answer: RDS Multi-AZ provides synchronous replication to a standby in another AZ with near-zero RPO — only seconds of data loss in a failover. Aurora Global Database replicates to a secondary region with RPO typically under 1 second. For the highest resiliency, combine RDS Multi-AZ within a region with Aurora Global DB cross-region, and supplement with automated backups and point-in-time recovery (PITR) for protection against logical corruption.

questions.question: How does Multivalue Answer routing differ from Failover routing? Why would you pick one over the other?
questions.answer: Failover routing is active-passive — it routes all traffic to a primary resource and only switches to a secondary if the primary fails. It enforces a hierarchy. Multivalue Answer is active-active — it returns up to 8 healthy IPs randomly per query and lets the client pick one. It distributes load across all healthy resources simultaneously. Choose Failover when you need a clear primary/backup DR setup. Choose Multivalue when you want simple DNS-level load distribution across multiple healthy resources without advanced routing logic.

questions.question: Describe a situation where you used Route 53 Weighted Routing to deploy a new application version safely.
questions.answer: (Situation) Our team needed to deploy a refactored payment service to production without risking a full outage if bugs emerged. (Task) We needed to release with minimal risk and fast rollback capability. (Action) We configured Route 53 Weighted Routing with two records pointing to the old and new ALB environments. We started with weights of 95 (old) and 5 (new), monitored CloudWatch error rates and latency for 30 minutes, then shifted to 80/20, then 50/50, then 0/100 over two hours. Auto Scaling handled the increasing load on the new environment. (Result) We detected a minor caching bug at the 10% stage affecting only 10% of users, set new environment weight to 0 to stop traffic instantly, patched it, and re-deployed successfully.

questions.question: A client in France reports their traffic is being routed to a US server instead of the EU server. How would you troubleshoot Route 53 routing policy configuration?
questions.answer: (Situation) EU users being routed incorrectly despite having EU servers configured. (Task) Diagnose and fix the misconfiguration. (Action) First, I would confirm the routing policy — if it's Geolocation, check that a record exists for Europe/France specifically, and that a default record is configured for unmatched locations. I'd use the Route 53 console's 'Test record set' feature to simulate a DNS query from a French IP. I'd also check if Geolocation vs Latency was the right policy choice — if the requirement is geographic compliance (GDPR), Geolocation is correct; if it's performance-based, Latency is correct. (Result) Found that the France/EU record was missing and only a default record existed, routing all traffic to US. Added EU geolocation record and verified with dig from a European resolver.

questions.question: How would you design a Route 53 architecture to achieve both low latency for global users and automatic failover if a region goes down?
questions.answer: (Situation) Global application in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 with reliability and performance requirements. (Task) Design DNS routing that optimises performance and handles regional failures. (Action) Implement Latency routing policy so users are directed to the nearest low-latency region normally. Attach Route 53 health checks to each regional ALB endpoint. Configure Route 53 to automatically exclude unhealthy regions from Latency routing responses. For each region, back it with RDS Multi-AZ for database resilience. Enable CloudWatch alarms tied to health check status for alerting. (Result) Users get lowest-latency routing under normal conditions. If us-east-1 ALB fails health checks, all traffic automatically shifts to eu-west-1 — no manual intervention. Combines the benefits of Latency routing with health-check-driven failover.

questions.question: Walk me through how you would execute a Blue/Green deployment for a major feature release using AWS services.
questions.answer: (Situation) Major feature release for an EC2-based web application requiring zero-downtime deployment with instant rollback. (Task) Deploy safely with full pre-production validation. (Action) 1. Provision Green environment (new version) with same EC2 capacity as Blue, behind a new ALB. 2. Run full regression and load tests against Green's ALB directly (no user traffic). 3. In Route 53, keep Blue at weight 100, add Green at weight 0. 4. When tests pass, switch Route 53 to point 100% traffic from Blue ALB to Green ALB (update A/CNAME record or switch weighted record to Green=100, Blue=0). 5. Monitor Green for 15–30 minutes. 6. If issues arise, instantly switch back to Blue by updating Route 53. 7. After confidence, terminate Blue environment. (Result) Zero-downtime deployment with instant rollback capability during the release window.

questions.question: A startup needs to show different landing pages to users in Japan, UK, and the USA. How would you configure Route 53?
questions.answer: (Situation) Region-specific landing pages for three markets. (Task) Route users to country-specific servers based on their location. (Action) Create a public hosted zone for the domain. Create three A records all for the same domain name (e.g., www.example.com) with routing policy set to Geolocation. Record 1: Location = Japan → Japanese server IP. Record 2: Location = United Kingdom → UK server IP. Record 3: Location = United States → US server IP. Add a fourth default record pointing to a global server to handle any unmatched locations. Attach health checks to each record so traffic automatically redirects if a regional server goes down. (Result) Japanese users see Japanese content, UK users see UK content, and US users see US content — with automatic failover if any region becomes unhealthy.

questions.question: Explain why TTL management is critical before a DNS migration and what happens if you ignore it.
questions.answer: (Situation) Migrating a high-traffic website from one hosting provider to another. (Task) Ensure smooth DNS cutover with minimal disruption. (Action) Two weeks before migration, lower TTL from 86400 seconds (24 hours) to 300 seconds (5 minutes). On migration day, update DNS records to point to new servers. Because TTL is 300 seconds, all resolvers worldwide will pick up the new IP within 5 minutes. If you ignored TTL, resolvers that cached the old 86400-second TTL would still serve the old IP for up to 24 hours — some users would reach the old server, others the new one, creating split-brain issues and partial outages. (Result) With low TTL, migration was visible globally within 5–10 minutes; rollback was equally fast if needed.

questions.question: Your team deployed a canary at 10% traffic but the new version has a 500% increase in database query errors. What do you do and what does this demonstrate about canary strategy?
questions.answer: (Situation) Canary at 10% shows severe database errors not seen in staging. (Task) Minimise user impact and resolve the issue. (Action) Immediately set the new environment's weighted routing record to 0 — stopping all canary traffic within the next TTL expiry (keep TTL low during deployments for faster response). Investigate: check CloudWatch logs, RDS metrics, and application logs in the new environment. Root cause: a new ORM version generated inefficient N+1 queries at scale that staging's low traffic didn't expose. Fix the query optimisation, re-deploy to the new environment, and restart the canary at 5%. (Result) Only 10% of users experienced the issue briefly. This demonstrates the core advantage of canary deployments — real production traffic reveals bugs that staging misses, and the small blast radius limits user impact.

questions.question: What is the SLA for Route 53 availability, and why is it significant compared to other AWS services?
questions.answer: Route 53 provides a 100% availability SLA — one of the very few AWS services with this guarantee. This is significant because DNS is foundational to all internet connectivity. If Route 53 were unavailable, users couldn't resolve any domain names to reach your application at all, even if all your EC2 instances and databases were perfectly healthy. The 100% SLA reflects that Route 53 is built on a globally distributed, redundant infrastructure of name servers in multiple Availability Zones and regions worldwide.

questions.question: When would you choose Aurora Global Database over RDS Multi-AZ from an RPO/RTO perspective?
questions.answer: Choose RDS Multi-AZ when your disaster recovery requirement is within the same AWS Region — it provides automatic failover to a standby in another AZ within 60–120 seconds (excellent RTO) with synchronous replication (near-zero RPO within the region). Choose Aurora Global Database when your RPO/RTO requirements span across AWS Regions — it replicates to a secondary region with RPO typically under 1 second and can promote the secondary region to primary with RTO typically under 1 minute. Aurora Global DB is the right choice when you need to survive a full regional outage, not just an AZ-level failure.

questions.question: Explain how Route 53 health checks work and what happens when a health check fails during Failover routing.
questions.answer: Route 53 health checks periodically probe your endpoint (HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP) from multiple AWS locations. You configure the protocol, port, path, interval (10 or 30 seconds), and failure threshold (how many consecutive failures before marking unhealthy). When a health check fails the threshold, Route 53 marks the associated DNS record as unhealthy. In Failover routing: if the primary record becomes unhealthy, Route 53 automatically stops returning the primary IP and starts returning the secondary record's IP in DNS responses. New DNS queries (and queries after TTL expiry) resolve to the secondary. Once the primary recovers and the health check passes, Route 53 resumes returning the primary IP.

questions.question: Design a multi-region disaster recovery architecture on AWS that achieves an RPO of under 1 minute and RTO of under 5 minutes.
questions.answer: To achieve RPO < 1 minute and RTO < 5 minutes across regions: Database layer — use Aurora Global Database with a secondary region replica (RPO ~1 second cross-region). Compute layer — use EC2 Auto Scaling groups in both primary and secondary regions, with AMIs pre-baked and launch templates ready in the secondary region. Traffic layer — use Route 53 Failover routing with health checks on both regions' ALBs. Set health check interval to 10 seconds with a failure threshold of 2 (unhealthy declared in 20 seconds). Application state — use ElastiCache with cross-region replication or design stateless application tier backed by DynamoDB Global Tables. Monitoring — CloudWatch alarms notify operations within 1 minute of health check failure. At failure: Route 53 automatically diverts traffic to secondary region ALB (within 20–30 seconds of failure). Aurora secondary is promoted (under 1 minute). The combined system achieves RPO ~1 second (Aurora) and RTO ~2–3 minutes (Route 53 failover + secondary region warm-up).

questions.question: Explain the trade-offs between using Route 53 Latency routing vs a CDN like CloudFront for improving global application performance.
questions.answer: Latency routing and CloudFront solve different performance problems. Route 53 Latency routing directs the initial DNS query to the AWS Region with the lowest latency — the user then connects directly to that region's origin server. Every user request still traverses the internet to the origin. CloudFront places cached content at 400+ edge locations worldwide — users connect to the nearest edge, which serves cached content without hitting the origin at all. The combination is most powerful: use Latency routing to direct CloudFront origin requests to the nearest low-latency region, while CloudFront serves cached content to users from its global edge network. Latency routing optimises origin selection; CloudFront eliminates the origin round-trip for cacheable content.

questions.question: How would you architect a zero-downtime database migration using Route 53 and weighted routing?
questions.answer: Zero-downtime database migration strategy: Phase 1 — Set up dual-write. Application writes to both old and new database simultaneously. New database is in sync. Phase 2 — Validate. Run read traffic against new database at 0% (just the dual-write sync) and verify data integrity. Phase 3 — Gradual read migration. Configure Route 53 Weighted Routing to split read traffic: 95% old DB, 5% new DB. Monitor error rates, query latency, and data correctness. Increase new DB weight gradually: 10%, 25%, 50%, 100%. Phase 4 — Write cutover. Once 100% reads are on new DB with confidence, perform a brief write cutover (maintenance window or dual-write cutover). Phase 5 — Decommission. Stop dual-write. Decommission old database. At each phase, weighted routing provides instant rollback by setting new DB weight to 0.

questions.question: What is the difference between Geolocation and Geoproximity routing in Route 53?
questions.answer: Geolocation routing routes based on the user's geographic location — continent, country, or US state. You define fixed rules: users from Germany go to EU, users from Japan go to Asia. The boundaries are fixed. Geoproximity routing (available within Route 53 Traffic Flow) routes based on the geographic proximity of users to resources, with a configurable bias parameter that expands or shrinks the area each resource serves. A positive bias on a resource captures more surrounding traffic; a negative bias pushes traffic away. Geoproximity is more flexible and dynamic — you can shift traffic boundaries without changing user locations. It's more complex to configure and requires Route 53 Traffic Flow. For most exam scenarios, Geolocation is the tested policy.

questions.question: You are designing the DNS strategy for a SaaS platform that needs to serve 10 million users globally with high availability. What Route 53 architecture would you recommend?
questions.answer: For a globally distributed, highly available SaaS platform: 1. Use CloudFront as the primary content delivery layer — 400+ edge locations serve static and cacheable content with low latency. 2. Configure Route 53 Latency routing to direct API/dynamic requests to the nearest AWS Region (e.g., us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1) for lowest origin latency. 3. Attach Route 53 health checks to each region's ALB — if a region fails health checks, Latency routing automatically excludes it, effectively acting as failover. 4. Use Aurora Global Database across all three regions for near-zero RPO (under 1 second) with ability to promote a secondary in under 1 minute (near-zero RTO). 5. Use DynamoDB Global Tables for session and metadata storage — multi-active with near-zero RPO globally. 6. Set DNS TTL to 60 seconds for faster propagation of routing changes. 7. Use Route 53 health checks with 10-second intervals and threshold of 2 for 20-second failure detection. This architecture provides: global low-latency (Latency routing + CloudFront), automatic regional failover (health checks), near-zero RPO/RTO (Aurora Global + DynamoDB Global Tables), and supports 10M+ users with Auto Scaling in each region.
